seo.meta_title: How to Say 'I Love It' in Korean | Not Always '사랑해요'
seo.meta_description: 'I love this coffee' isn't 이 커피 사랑해요 in everyday Korean. How Koreans say they love food, places and hobbies — 좋아해요, 최고예요 and more.

ai_failure.situation: Your Korean coworker brings you a pastry from a local bakery, and you want to say 'I love this!'
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Translates 'I love it' as 이거 사랑해요.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: 사랑하다 is a heavy word, used for people, family and deep devotion. Saying it about a pastry sounds like an ad slogan or an over-the-top joke rather than a natural reaction.

natural_solution.rule: For things you like, use 좋아해요 (I like it, in general) or react to the thing itself: 너무 맛있어요, 진짜 좋아요, 최고예요.

alternatives.context: Reacting to food you're eating right now
Saying you love something in general
Loving a place, a café, an outfit — casual-polite

nuance: English uses 'love' for everything from a partner to a sandwich. Korean keeps 사랑하다 mostly for people and deep attachments, and switches to 좋아하다 ('like') for food, hobbies and places — even when the feeling is strong. You'll still hear playful exaggerations like 떡볶이 사랑해! among friends or in advertising, but as a default, describing the thing (맛있다, 예쁘다, 최고다) sounds far more natural.
